find: A private contractor petitions a state court to enjoin a former employee from publishing a critical op-ed in breach of a voluntary settlement's non-disparagement clause. The employee cites \textit{Shelley}, claiming judicial enforcement triggers First Amendment strict scrutiny. Although \textit{Shelley}'s broad language invites the argument, modern courts reject extending its attribution rationale to private speech contracts (\textit{United Egg Producers}), preserving private ordering under \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/587/17-1702/}{\textit{Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck}, 587 U.S. 802 (2019)}, while confining judicial state action to racial discrimination or core courtroom processes such as peremptory strikes (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/500/614/}{\textit{Edmonson v. Leesville Concrete Co.}, 500 U.S. 614 (1991)}).
replace: A private contractor sues in state court for actual damages after a former employee publishes a critical op-ed in breach of a specific, voluntary non-disparagement provision in their settlement. The former employee argues that judicial enforcement automatically triggers strict scrutiny. Under \textit{Cohen v.\ Cowles Media Co.}, 501 U.S.\ 663 (1991), judicial application of state law can constitute state action, while a damages claim enforcing a voluntarily assumed obligation under generally applicable law need not violate the First Amendment. The damages claim may proceed on these facts, subject to applicable limits on enforcement of the agreement.
reason: Cohen expressly recognized state action and upheld damages under a generally applicable rule. Halleck's rule for private forum operators does not limit judicial state action. Cohen did not approve a prospective injunction against publication.
